title: Waiting in line
hook: The Buddha remembers sitting as a boy in a rose-apple tree's shade, and finds the way
tomorrow: what did an emperor tell himself in the morning about rude people?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the well: plain days, worship with no mountain. This week's lines come back in the games today: kindness stays, prepared, presence, for after, no quarrel, plain days. And one more plain place.
screen: `PLAIN DAYS.` → `A WEEK OF LINES COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: The pharmacy line hasn't moved in ages. Everyone's staring at a phone. The Buddha told a story about himself that starts somewhere like this, in a stuck place. Before his awakening he had been starving himself, trying to force a breakthrough, and it wasn't coming. Then a memory surfaced. As a boy, while his father was busy at work, he had sat in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, and a quiet, happy stillness had come over him all on its own. Nobody asked anything of him. He was just sitting. Could that, he wondered, be the way?
screen: `THE LINE ISN'T MOVING.` → `FORCING IT ISN'T WORKING.` → `A BOY IN THE ROSE-APPLE SHADE.` → `COULD THAT BE THE WAY?`

segments.voice: In the Pali Canon he tells what came next: with the memory came a knowing, that is the way. Then he asked himself why he was afraid of that kind of happiness, one that has nothing to do with craving, and decided he wasn't. He ate again and stopped the war with his own body. Buddhists call the path that followed the middle way, between indulging and grinding. And some teachers link that stillness in the shade to a practice he later taught, anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing: breathing in, knowing you breathe in; breathing out, knowing you breathe out. A queue is a little rose-apple shade. Nothing's being asked of you but to wait, and the breath is right there. Not forcing calm. Not scrolling to escape. Just in, and knowing it. Out, and knowing it. This path borrows that practice, with its source named, for every line you'll ever stand in.
screen: `THAT IS THE WAY.` · `NOT AFRAID OF THAT HAPPINESS.` · `THE MIDDLE WAY.` · `BREATHING IN, KNOWING IT.` · then, large: `THE QUEUE.`

segments.voice: Stand up if you can, the way you'd stand in a line: weight on both feet, hands loose. Breathe in, and know you're breathing in. Breathe out, and know you're breathing out, until the bell.
Waiting in line: a plain wait where the boy's shade comes back. Breathing in, knowing it; breathing out, knowing it.
Your line: the queue, a little shade to breathe in. Two of fourteen, and a week of lines gathered.

howItsDone: Buddhists practice anapanasati, knowing each breath as it comes in and goes out; people on this path borrow it for lines and waits, standing quietly instead of scrolling.

fork.setup: your coworker says waiting is wasted time, so she answers emails in every line. what fits the rose-apple shade?
options: a wait can be the shade: nothing asked of you but to breathe and know it.
she's right: the Buddha taught never to let a single minute go to waste.

fork.reveal: the Buddha's way opened when he remembered a boy just waiting in the shade. the breath practice he taught asks only that you know each breath.

chat.says: pharmacy line for Edie's meds. not moving at all. i'm about to lose it.
options: do what the Buddha remembered from the shade: breathe in, know it; breathe out, know it.
force yourself calm: the Buddha got there by grinding it out, so grit your teeth.

chat.meaning: The Buddha found the way by remembering an effortless stillness in the shade, not by forcing. Knowing each breath turns a wait into that shade.

tie.story: After forcing got nowhere, the Buddha remembered a boyhood stillness under a rose-apple tree and knew: that is the way.
tie.friend: Zoe can stand in the pharmacy line and know each breath instead of fighting the wait.

Buddha.meaning: the awakened one, who founded Buddhism

rose-apple.meaning: a shade tree of India with fragrant fruit

Pali Canon.meaning: the early Buddhist scriptures, kept in the Pali language

anapanasati.meaning: mindfulness of breathing in and out

middle way.meaning: the Buddha's path between indulging and harsh self-denial

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 36, Mahasaccaka Sutta (the memory of the rose-apple shade; 'that is the way'; not afraid of that happiness; taking food again)
